about: How to turn on hybrid post-quantum key exchange (X25519MLKEM768) for each stack that can serve a public HTTPS host. Every recipe was checked against the vendor's own documentation on the date in its sources. Nothing here is a guess: where the vendor documents no support, the recipe says so and gives the honest next step.

cloudflare.name: Cloudflare
cloudflare.summary: Cloudflare offers X25519MLKEM768 to visitors on every proxied hostname over TLS 1.3. There is no switch to turn it on.
cloudflare.snippet_label: Nothing to enable. If this host still negotiates a classical group, check these two settings
cloudflare.snippet:
# 1. DNS > Records: the record for this hostname must be Proxied (orange cloud), not DNS only.
# 2. SSL/TLS > Edge Certificates > TLS 1.3 must be On. The same setting through the API:
curl -X PATCH "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/zones/$ZONE_ID/settings/tls_1_3" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CF_API_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{"value":"on"}'
requires: The hostname proxied through Cloudflare (orange cloud)
TLS 1.3 on for the zone
stays_classical_if: the DNS record is DNS only (grey cloud), so visitors reach your own server, not Cloudflare
TLS 1.3 is switched off for the zone: Cloudflare offers post-quantum key agreement only over TLS 1.3
the visitor's own client has no post-quantum support
cloudflare.origin_note: Cloudflare to your origin: Automatic key exchange is on by default (SSL/TLS > Overview > Origin connection & post-quantum encryption). That leg is post-quantum only when your origin also offers X25519MLKEM768: see the nginx, Apache, HAProxy or Caddy recipe.

sources.title: Cloudflare: Post-quantum cryptography
sources.quote: As of October 2022, all websites and APIs served through Cloudflare over TLS 1.3 support post-quantum hybrid key agreement.

sources.title: Cloudflare: Post-quantum in Cloudflare products
sources.quote: Visitor key agreement: X25519MLKEM768, for any proxied hostname or HTTPS application behind Cloudflare.

sources.title: Cloudflare: Post-quantum to origins
sources.quote: Automatic key exchange is on for all existing zones and on by default for new zones.

cloudfront.name: Amazon CloudFront
cloudfront.summary: CloudFront offers hybrid post-quantum key establishment on every TLS security policy, automatically, for visitor connections over TLS 1.3.
cloudfront.snippet_label: Nothing to enable. To confirm which distribution answers for this host
requires: The hostname served by a CloudFront distribution
A visitor client using TLS 1.3
stays_classical_if: the hostname is not actually served by CloudFront (check the DNS record points at the distribution)
the visitor's client uses TLS 1.2: CloudFront supports quantum-safe key exchange only with TLS 1.3
cloudfront.origin_note: AWS documents no post-quantum setting for the CloudFront-to-origin leg.

sources.title: AWS What's New: CloudFront post-quantum support
sources.quote: support for hybrid post-quantum key establishment across all existing Transport Layer Security (TLS) security policies

sources.title: CloudFront: Supported protocols and ciphers between viewers and CloudFront
sources.quote: Quantum-safe key exchanges are only supported with TLS 1.3.

aws_elb.name: AWS Application or Network Load Balancer
aws_elb.summary: Elastic Load Balancing offers hybrid post-quantum key exchange only on security policies with PQ in their name. The CLI and CloudFormation default (ELBSecurityPolicy-2016-08) is classical.
aws_elb.snippet_label: Switch the HTTPS (ALB) or TLS (NLB) listener to a PQ security policy
aws_elb.snippet:
# Find the listener
aws elbv2 describe-listeners --load-balancer-arn <load-balancer-arn>
# Move it to a policy with PQ in its name
aws elbv2 modify-listener --listener-arn <listener-arn> \
  --ssl-policy ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-Res-PQ-2025-09
requires: A security policy whose name contains PQ, for example ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-Res-PQ-2025-09
stays_classical_if: the listener still uses a policy without PQ in its name
the visitor's client does not support ML-KEM
aws_elb.notes: All secure listeners on one load balancer must use compatible policies, and AWS lists PQ and non-PQ policies as not compatible: move every HTTPS or TLS listener on the load balancer, following AWS's guide. The console's default for new listeners is already a PQ policy; the CLI, CloudFormation and CDK default is not.

sources.title: ALB: Security policies
sources.quote: Security policies with PQ in their names offer hybrid post-quantum key exchange ... support SecP256r1MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024 and X25519MLKEM768.

sources.title: NLB: Security policies
sources.quote: Security policies with PQ in their names offer hybrid post-quantum key exchange.

sources.title: ALB: Update an HTTPS listener
sources.quote: aws elbv2 modify-listener --listener-arn listener-arn --ssl-policy policy-name

aws_apigateway.name: Amazon API Gateway (REST API custom domain)
aws_apigateway.summary: API Gateway offers hybrid post-quantum key exchange on security policies with PQ in their name, for REST APIs on Regional or private custom domains only. Edge-optimized endpoints and HTTP or WebSocket APIs have no PQ policy.
aws_apigateway.snippet_label: Move the custom domain to a PQ security policy (takes about 15 minutes)
requires: A REST API on a Regional or private custom domain
A security policy whose name contains PQ
stays_classical_if: the API is edge-optimized, or is an HTTP or WebSocket API: AWS offers no PQ policy for these
the custom domain still uses TLS_1_0 or TLS_1_2
aws_apigateway.notes: AWS's page says hybrid key exchange without naming the group. A domain on these policies cannot use mutual TLS or have HTTP APIs mapped to it. AWS suggests the BASIC endpoint access mode first and STRICT once traffic checks out.

sources.title: API Gateway: Supported security policies
sources.quote: Policies that contain PQ in the title use Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) to implement hybrid key exchange algorithms.

sources.title: API Gateway: Choose a security policy for a custom domain
sources.quote: aws apigateway update-domain-name --domain-name example.com --patch-operations ...

azure_front_door.name: Azure Front Door
azure_front_door.summary: Azure Front Door (Standard and Premium) offers X25519MLKEM768 under its default Standard key exchange policy, over TLS 1.3. No action is needed unless the policy was changed.
azure_front_door.snippet_label: Nothing to enable. If this host still negotiates a classical group
azure_front_door.snippet:
# In the Azure portal, open the Front Door profile and the custom domain for this host.
# Set its TLS key exchange policy back to Standard (the default).
# Enhanced has no X25519-based groups, and a Custom policy may leave the hybrid groups out.
requires: Azure Front Door Standard or Premium
The Standard key exchange policy (the default)
TLS 1.3
stays_classical_if: the key exchange policy is Enhanced, or Custom without the hybrid groups
the connection is TLS 1.2: hybrid methods require TLS 1.3
the visitor's client supports no hybrid group
azure_front_door.origin_note: This covers the visitor-to-Front Door leg only, not Front Door to your origin.

sources.title: Azure Front Door: TLS key exchange policy
sources.quote: Standard is the default key exchange policy for new and existing profiles.

sources.title: Microsoft: Azure Front Door supports post-quantum resilient hybrid TLS 1.3
sources.quote: TLS 1.3 hybrid PQC is enabled by default; no customer action is required.

azure_app_gateway.name: Azure Application Gateway
azure_app_gateway.summary: Microsoft documents no post-quantum key exchange for Application Gateway: its TLS policies cover protocol versions and cipher suites only. There is no setting to copy.
azure_app_gateway.snippet_label: No vendor setting exists yet. The honest next step
azure_app_gateway.snippet:
# Option 1: put Azure Front Door in front of the Application Gateway. Front Door's default
#           Standard key exchange policy offers X25519MLKEM768 to visitors.
# Option 2: ask Microsoft (support case) when Application Gateway will offer ML-KEM.
stays_classical_if: visitors connect to Application Gateway directly

sources.title: Application Gateway: TLS policy overview
sources.quote: No mention of ML-KEM, post-quantum or key-exchange groups as of the date checked.

google_lb.name: Google Cloud Load Balancing
google_lb.summary: Google Cloud's external and internal Application Load Balancers and proxy Network Load Balancers offer X25519MLKEM768 through the post-quantum-key-exchange setting of an SSL policy. Google said it would begin enabling it by default in October 2026; setting ENABLED is the sure way.
google_lb.snippet_label: Turn it on in the SSL policy attached to the load balancer's target proxy
google_lb.snippet:
# Already have an SSL policy on the target proxy (add --region REGION for a regional one):
gcloud compute ssl-policies update SSL_POLICY_NAME --post-quantum-key-exchange ENABLED

# No SSL policy yet: create one and attach it
gcloud compute ssl-policies create SSL_POLICY_NAME --profile MODERN --min-tls-version 1.2 \
  --post-quantum-key-exchange ENABLED
gcloud compute target-https-proxies update TARGET_HTTPS_PROXY_NAME --ssl-policy SSL_POLICY_NAME
requires: An external or internal Application Load Balancer, or a proxy Network Load Balancer
An SSL policy with post-quantum-key-exchange ENABLED
stays_classical_if: the SSL policy is DEFERRED, or DEFAULT before Google's switch-over
the host is served by Google's front end without Cloud Load Balancing (for example a default Cloud Run or Firebase address): Google documents no setting there
the visitor's client lacks TLS 1.3 or X25519MLKEM768
google_lb.notes: Detection by Google's front-end headers cannot tell Cloud Load Balancing from other Google-hosted services. This applies to client connections only, not to backends.

sources.title: Google Cloud: Post-quantum TLS for load balancers
sources.quote: Google Cloud will begin enabling it by default in October 2026.

sources.title: Google Cloud: Use SSL policies
sources.quote: gcloud compute ssl-policies update SSL_POLICY_NAME ... --post-quantum-key-exchange MODE

fastly.name: Fastly
fastly.summary: Fastly says customers on TLS 1.3 get post-quantum key exchange automatically, with no action needed. This comes from Fastly's announcement; its documentation does not yet describe it.
fastly.snippet_label: Nothing to enable. If this host still negotiates a classical group
fastly.snippet:
# Fastly documents no setting to copy. Check that the service's TLS configuration allows TLS 1.3,
# then ask Fastly support whether post-quantum key exchange is live for this hostname.
requires: TLS 1.3 on the Fastly TLS configuration
stays_classical_if: the TLS configuration does not allow TLS 1.3
the rollout does not yet cover this hostname: Fastly's announcement does not say when it finished

sources.title: Fastly: Future-proofing TLS encryption against quantum threats
sources.quote: TLS 1.3 customers will automatically benefit from post-quantum key exchange with no required action.

akamai.name: Akamai
akamai.summary: Akamai's Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC) Client to Edge behavior is on by default for Enhanced TLS and Standard TLS hostnames, when the certificate has TLS 1.3 enabled.
akamai.snippet_label: If this host still negotiates a classical group: the Property Manager behavior (rule tree JSON)
requires: The behavior Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC) Client to Edge on
TLS 1.3 enabled on the certificate
stays_classical_if: the PQC Client to Edge behavior is set to Off in the property
TLS 1.3 is not enabled in the certificate's deployment settings
akamai.origin_note: Akamai to your origin: the behavior Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC) to Origin is off by default and needs a TLS 1.3 origin of type Your Origin with SNI on.
akamai.notes: Akamai's own pages disagree on scope: the Terraform reference says Enhanced TLS hostnames only, the Property Manager page (2 Nov 2026) includes Standard TLS.

sources.title: Akamai: PQC Client to Edge
sources.quote: is enabled by default for all Enhanced TLS and Standard TLS hostnames

sources.title: Akamai: PQC to Origin
sources.quote: is disabled by default.

nginx.name: nginx
nginx.summary: nginx hands the key-exchange list to OpenSSL. With OpenSSL 3.5 or newer, X25519MLKEM768 is in OpenSSL's default list, so nginx's default (ssl_ecdh_curve auto) already offers it; an explicit list without it, or an older OpenSSL, is the usual cause.
nginx.snippet_label: In the http { } or server { } block that terminates TLS
nginx.snippet:
# 1. nginx must be linked against OpenSSL 3.5 or newer:
nginx -V 2>&1 | grep -i openssl
# 2. Offer the hybrid group first:
ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;
ssl_ecdh_curve X25519MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1:secp384r1;
# 3. Test, then reload:
nginx -t && nginx -s reload
requires: nginx 1.11.0 or newer (curve lists)
OpenSSL 3.5.0 or newer
stays_classical_if: nginx is linked against OpenSSL older than 3.5: the group name is then rejected and nginx will not start, so check nginx -V first
another server block or an included file sets ssl_ecdh_curve without X25519MLKEM768

sources.title: nginx: ngx_http_ssl_module, ssl_ecdh_curve
sources.quote: The special value auto (1.11.0) instructs nginx to use a list built into the OpenSSL library

sources.title: OpenSSL 3.5.0 NEWS
sources.quote: The default TLS supported groups list has been changed to include and prefer hybrid PQC KEM groups.

apache.name: Apache httpd
apache.summary: mod_ssl passes the Groups command straight to OpenSSL. With OpenSSL 3.5 or newer, X25519MLKEM768 is in the default list; set it explicitly if your configuration names its own groups.
apache.snippet_label: In the global mod_ssl configuration or the <VirtualHost *:443>
apache.snippet:
# mod_ssl normally uses the system OpenSSL; it must be 3.5 or newer:
#   openssl version
SSLProtocol -all +TLSv1.2 +TLSv1.3
SSLOpenSSLConfCmd Groups X25519MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1:secp384r1
# Test, then reload:
#   apachectl configtest && apachectl graceful
requires: Apache httpd 2.4.8 or newer (SSLOpenSSLConfCmd)
mod_ssl linked against OpenSSL 3.5.0 or newer
stays_classical_if: mod_ssl is linked against OpenSSL older than 3.5
another SSLOpenSSLConfCmd Groups or Curves line overrides this one

sources.title: Apache httpd: mod_ssl, SSLOpenSSLConfCmd
sources.quote: Available in httpd 2.4.8 and later, if using OpenSSL 1.0.2 or later

sources.title: OpenSSL 3.5: SSL_CONF_cmd, Groups
sources.quote: Groups: This sets the supported groups. ... Curves: This is a synonym for the "Groups" command.

sources.title: OpenSSL 3.5: SSL_CTX_set1_curves
sources.quote: The DEFAULT list selects X25519MLKEM768 as one of the predicted keyshares.

haproxy.name: HAProxy
haproxy.summary: HAProxy passes its curve list to the TLS library it was built with. HAProxy Technologies says Enterprise 3.2+ and Community 3.3+ support hybrid post-quantum key exchange natively in their AWS-LC builds; a build linked against OpenSSL 3.5 or newer can offer it too.
haproxy.snippet_label: In the global section (or the curves option on each bind line)
haproxy.snippet:
# Check the TLS library first (AWS-LC, or OpenSSL 3.5+):
#   haproxy -vv | grep -i -e openssl -e aws-lc
global
    ssl-default-bind-options ssl-min-ver TLSv1.2
    ssl-default-bind-curves X25519MLKEM768:X25519:P-256:P-384
# Test, then reload:
#   haproxy -c -f /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg
requires: HAProxy 2.2 or newer (ssl-default-bind-curves)
A TLS library with ML-KEM: AWS-LC, or OpenSSL 3.5.0 or newer
stays_classical_if: the binary is linked against a TLS library without ML-KEM
a bind line sets its own curves without X25519MLKEM768

sources.title: HAProxy: How to enable post-quantum cryptography
sources.quote: HAProxy Enterprise 3.2+ and HAProxy Community 3.3+ support hybrid post-quantum cryptography natively

sources.title: HAProxy 3.2 configuration manual: curves
sources.quote: It sets the string describing the list of elliptic curves algorithms ("curve suite") that are negotiated during the SSL/TLS handshake with ECDHE.

caddy.name: Caddy
caddy.summary: Caddy 2.10 and newer (built with Go 1.24+) offer x25519mlkem768 by default. The fix is to upgrade Caddy and remove any curves override.
caddy.snippet_label: Upgrade to Caddy 2.10+, then delete any curves line. The explicit form, if you must set one
requires: Caddy 2.10.0 or newer (built with Go 1.24 or newer)
stays_classical_if: Caddy is older than 2.10
a tls block sets curves without x25519mlkem768

sources.title: Caddy v2.10.0 release notes
sources.quote: Caddy now supports the standardized x25519mlkem768 cryptographic group by default.

sources.title: Caddyfile: tls directive
sources.quote: It is recommended to not change the defaults

traefik.name: Traefik
traefik.summary: Traefik 3.5 and newer are built with Go 1.24, whose TLS default includes X25519MLKEM768. Upgrade, and if you set curvePreferences, put X25519MLKEM768 first.
traefik.snippet_label: Dynamic configuration (file provider). Leave curvePreferences unset, or
traefik.snippet:
tls:
  options:
    default:
      curvePreferences:
        - X25519MLKEM768
        - X25519
        - CurveP256
requires: Traefik 3.5.0 or newer (Go 1.24)
stays_classical_if: Traefik is older than 3.5
curvePreferences is set without X25519MLKEM768
GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=0 is set in the environment
traefik.notes: Traefik's documentation does not list X25519MLKEM768; the value is in Traefik's source from v3.5.0. TLS options cannot be set through label or tag based providers.

sources.title: Go crypto/tls (1.24): Config.CurvePreferences
sources.quote: From Go 1.24, the default includes the X25519MLKEM768 hybrid post-quantum key exchange.

sources.title: Traefik: TLS options
sources.quote: TLS options are not supported by label or tag-based providers.

iis.name: IIS (Windows Schannel)
iis.summary: Windows Schannel offers hybrid ML-KEM on Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 24H2 or later with a current update, but it is off by default. Windows Server 2022 and earlier have no ML-KEM in Schannel.
iis.snippet_label: Elevated PowerShell on the server, then restart
iis.snippet:
Enable-TlsEccCurve -Name "X25519_MLKEM768" -Position 0
Get-TlsEccCurve   # X25519_MLKEM768 should be listed first
Restart-Computer
requires: Windows Server 2025 (or Windows 11 24H2+) with a current cumulative update: Microsoft lists the minimum builds
TLS 1.3
stays_classical_if: the server runs Windows Server 2022 or earlier: put a post-quantum capable proxy or CDN in front of IIS
a Group Policy ECC Curve Order overrides the local setting
legacy FIPS mode is on: the hybrid groups are not available there
iis.notes: Microsoft's pages disagree on the exact minimum build and update, so check your build against Microsoft's list before relying on it.

sources.title: Microsoft: ASP.NET Kestrel and Schannel GA with TLS 1.3 post-quantum cryptography
sources.quote: the PQC groups are not enabled by default

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: TLS supported groups in Windows 11 24H2 and later
sources.quote: These groups are disabled by default, and must be enabled using one of the configuration methods linked at the end of this article.

unknown.name: Not identified
unknown.summary: Morrow could not tell what terminates TLS for this host, so it will not guess a setting. Pick your stack below if you know it.
unknown.snippet:
# 1. Find what terminates TLS for this host: your web server, load balancer or CDN.
# 2. If it is a managed service, ask the provider whether it offers X25519MLKEM768 and how to turn it on.
# 3. If it offers none, put a post-quantum capable proxy or CDN in front of it
#    (for example nginx or HAProxy with OpenSSL 3.5+, Caddy 2.10+, or a CDN that offers it by default).

config_recipes_about: Recipes for configuration files that are not a public HTTPS stack (pasted on the home page): OpenSSH, the OpenSSL configuration file and Java. Same rules as the recipes above: every claim names the vendor source and the date it was checked.

openssh.name: OpenSSH (sshd_config / ssh_config)
openssh.summary: OpenSSH 10.0 and newer use the hybrid mlkem768x25519-sha256 key agreement by default; 9.9 offers it. A KexAlgorithms line that leaves it (and sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com, the hybrid default since 9.0) out turns the post-quantum key exchange off.
openssh.snippet:
# 1. Check the version: OpenSSH 9.9 or newer has mlkem768x25519-sha256
ssh -V
# 2. Put the hybrid methods first (or delete the KexAlgorithms line to use the default):
KexAlgorithms mlkem768x25519-sha256,sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com,curve25519-sha256,curve25519-sha256@libssh.org
# 3. Test, then reload:
sshd -t && systemctl reload sshd
requires: OpenSSH 9.9 or newer (mlkem768x25519-sha256); 10.0 or newer uses it by default
stays_classical_if: a KexAlgorithms line lists only classical methods (curve25519, ecdh-sha2-*, diffie-hellman-*)
the client is older than OpenSSH 9.0 and supports no hybrid method

sources.title: OpenSSH 10.0 release notes
sources.quote: the hybrid post-quantum algorithm mlkem768x25519-sha256 is now used by default for key agreement.

sources.title: OpenSSH 9.9 release notes
sources.quote: This algorithm "mlkem768x25519-sha256" is available by default.

openssl_cnf.name: OpenSSL configuration file (openssl.cnf)
openssl_cnf.summary: The system_default section sets the TLS defaults for every program that loads the OpenSSL configuration. With OpenSSL 3.5 or newer the built-in group list already prefers X25519MLKEM768; a Groups or Curves line without it, or an older OpenSSL, keeps the key exchange classical.
openssl_cnf.snippet_label: In the section that openssl_conf -> ssl_conf -> system_default points to
openssl_cnf.snippet:
# OpenSSL must be 3.5 or newer:
#   openssl version
openssl_conf = openssl_init

[openssl_init]
ssl_conf = ssl_sect

[ssl_sect]
system_default = system_default_sect

[system_default_sect]
MinProtocol = TLSv1.2
Groups = X25519MLKEM768:X25519:P-256:P-384
requires: OpenSSL 3.5.0 or newer
stays_classical_if: the program sets its own group list and ignores the system default
OpenSSL is older than 3.5: the group name is then rejected

sources.title: OpenSSL 3.5 SSL_CONF_cmd: Groups
sources.quote: This sets the supported groups. For clients, the groups are sent using the supported groups extension. For servers, it is used to determine which group to use.

sources.title: OpenSSL 3.5.0 NEWS
sources.quote: The default TLS supported groups list has been changed to include and prefer hybrid PQC KEM groups.

java.name: Java (java.security, JSSE)
java.summary: JDK 27 and newer put X25519MLKEM768 first in the TLS 1.3 named groups by default (JEP 527). Older JDKs have no hybrid TLS group, so the fix there is an upgrade. A jdk.tls.namedGroups setting without X25519MLKEM768 turns it off.
java.snippet_label: JDK 27 or newer; the system property only if you set your own list
java.snippet:
# 1. Check the runtime: JDK 27 or newer
java -version
# 2. If you set a named-groups list, put the hybrid group first:
-Djdk.tls.namedGroups=X25519MLKEM768,x25519,secp256r1,secp384r1
# 3. TLS 1.3 must stay enabled: do not list TLSv1.3 in jdk.tls.disabledAlgorithms
requires: JDK 27 or newer (JEP 527)
TLS 1.3
stays_classical_if: jdk.tls.namedGroups or SSLParameters.setNamedGroups lists only classical groups
the runtime is older than JDK 27

sources.title: JEP 527: Post-Quantum Hybrid Key Exchange for TLS 1.3
sources.quote: By default, the JDK’s TLS 1.3 implementation will place the X25519MLKEM768 hybrid scheme at the front of that list, making it the most preferred.
